items.prompt: For a closed-interval exact search on an array of length n, what are the usual initial boundaries?

options.text: left = 0 and right = n.
left = 0 and right = n - 1.
left = 1 and right = n.
left = -1 and right = n.

feedback.reason: A closed exact-search interval contains valid candidate indices from left through right.

blocks.text: A closed interval [left, right] includes both endpoints. An array of length n has valid indices 0 through n - 1, so left = 0 and right = n - 1 represent every candidate exactly once. For n = 0 this becomes [0, -1], already empty, and the ordinary loop condition prevents any array read.

blocks.title: Do not mix interval conventions
blocks.text: right = n belongs to a half-open [left, right) convention. Using it with closed-interval access and left <= right makes index n look like a real candidate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_n: Index n is outside a closed array interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_n: This skips index 0 and includes index n.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.minus_one_n: These are sentinels, not the ordinary active closed interval.

items.prompt: In ascending sorted data, nums[mid] is greater than target. Which closed-interval update preserves the exact-search invariant?

options.text: left = mid + 1.
right = mid.
right = mid - 1.
Return mid.

feedback.reason: Every index at or to the right of mid contains a value at least nums[mid], which is too large.

blocks.text: In ascending order, every index j >= mid satisfies nums[j] >= nums[mid] > target. Mid is known not to match, and neither can anything to its right. Setting right = mid - 1 removes exactly that proven-impossible region while retaining every possible target index on the left.

blocks.title: Why mid must leave
blocks.text: Strict inequality has already proved mid is not the target. Retaining right = mid weakens progress and does not match this closed any-match update.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_mid_plus_one: This discards the only side where a smaller target may remain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_mid: For exact search after strict greater-than, mid is known not to be the target and should be removed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_mid: The value at mid is not equal to target.

items.prompt: In ascending sorted data, nums[mid] is less than target. Which closed-interval update is correct?

options.text: right = mid - 1.
left = mid.
Return not found immediately.
left = mid + 1.

feedback.reason: Every index at or to the left of mid contains a value no greater than nums[mid], which is too small.

blocks.text: In ascending order, every index j <= mid satisfies nums[j] <= nums[mid] < target. The entire left region through mid is impossible. Setting left = mid + 1 preserves every remaining possible match and strictly reduces the closed interval.

blocks.title: The singleton progress check
blocks.text: If left = right = mid and nums[mid] is too small, left = mid would retain the same interval forever. left = mid + 1 removes the known nonmatch.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_mid_minus_one: This keeps only values that are no larger than nums[mid].
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_mid: Mid is known not to match and retaining it can prevent strict progress.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_not_found: The strict comparison rules out only mid and the left region; a matching target may still remain anywhere to the right.

items.prompt: What should an exact binary search do when nums[mid] equals target and the contract accepts any matching index?

options.text: Always continue left until the first occurrence.
Return mid immediately.
Always continue right until the last occurrence.
Discard mid and continue without recording it.

feedback.reason: The result contract is already satisfied by the matching midpoint.

blocks.text: The any-match output contract asks for one index whose value equals target. Once nums[mid] == target, mid is a complete witness and no remaining search can make it more valid. Continuing left or right is appropriate only after strengthening the objective to first or last occurrence.

blocks.title: Equality behavior belongs to the contract
blocks.text: Any-match returns immediately. First-match records mid and searches left; last-match records mid and searches right. These are different completion policies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.continue_left: That implements a lower-bound-style contract rather than any-match.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.continue_right: Searching right after equality implements a last-occurrence boundary policy that the any-match contract does not require.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.remove_mid: Discarding the matching midpoint without recording it can eliminate the only occurrence and turn a known hit into not found.

items.prompt: What should a correct closed-interval exact search return after the loop exits with left > right?

options.text: left is always a matching target index.
right is always a matching target index.
The target is not present in the searched array.
The last midpoint must be returned.

feedback.reason: The invariant says every possible target index remains inside [left, right].

blocks.text: Every mismatch removes only indices proven unable to match, so all possible target positions remain inside [left, right]. Exit with left > right means that closed interval contains zero indices. Because no equality branch returned earlier, the exact-search result is not found.

blocks.title: Insertion position is not an exact hit
blocks.text: After failure, left may be where target could be inserted while preserving order, but it is not necessarily an existing matching index and must not be returned as a hit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_index: For exact search, left may be only an insertion position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_index: The interval may be empty with no match.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_index: The last midpoint may contain a nonmatching value.

items.prompt: How should an iterative exact search behave on an empty array?

options.text: It reads index 0 once before returning.
It returns index 0 as the insertion point under the exact-index contract.
It must throw because binary search cannot represent emptiness.
The initial interval is empty, so it returns not found without reading an element.

feedback.reason: With left = 0 and right = -1, the loop condition left <= right is false.

blocks.text: For n = 0, initialization gives left = 0 and right = n - 1 = -1. The condition left <= right is false before midpoint computation, so the algorithm performs zero iterations, makes no array access, and returns not found through its normal empty-interval path.

blocks.title: No fabricated candidate
blocks.text: Index 0 is an insertion position in an empty array, but it is not a valid exact-match index. Empty input needs no sentinel element or fallback.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_zero: An empty array has no valid index 0, and the initially empty interval must prevent any midpoint access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_zero: The contract asks for a matching index, not insertion position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.throw_always: An empty interval is a normal searchable state.

items.prompt: A one-element array contains target. What should happen on the first iteration?

options.text: The loop is skipped because left equals right.
mid is 0, the value matches, and index 0 is returned.
right becomes -1 before the value is checked.
Index 1 is returned because length is 1.

feedback.reason: A singleton closed interval must be inspected.

blocks.text: For one element, initialization gives left = right = 0. Because a closed interval with equal endpoints contains one candidate, the loop condition must be left <= right. The midpoint is 0, equality satisfies the any-match contract, and index 0 is returned on that first iteration.

blocks.title: What left < right would break
blocks.text: Using left < right with a closed interval skips every singleton state, including a one-element input and the final candidate of a larger search.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_loop: A closed interval with left == right still contains one candidate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_negative: right changes only after comparing the existing candidate; preemptively setting -1 would discard the target without inspection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_one: Length 1 counts elements, while the sole valid zero-based index is 0; index 1 is out of bounds.

items.prompt: The sorted array contains duplicate target values, and the contract accepts any matching index. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The algorithm must return the first occurrence.
The algorithm must return the last occurrence.
Returning whichever matching midpoint is encountered is valid.
Duplicates make exact binary search incorrect.

feedback.reason: The invariant only needs to preserve the possibility of some target index.

blocks.text: Under an any-match contract, every index i with nums[i] == target is an equally valid witness. When the search encounters such a midpoint, returning it immediately is correct even if equal values also occur on either side. Duplicates require different equality behavior only for first-occurrence or last-occurrence objectives.

blocks.title: Do not infer a boundary objective
blocks.text: Continuing left or right after a match is not 'more correct' unless the prompt explicitly asks for an extreme duplicate position.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.must_first: That is not required by the stated contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.must_last: Last occurrence is a stronger boundary contract; it is not required when any equal index is accepted.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates_break_all: Duplicates do not invalidate equality or sorted-side elimination; they only make a specific duplicate boundary require extra logic.

items.prompt: Which midpoint formula avoids overflow in fixed-width integer arithmetic when left and right are nonnegative?
constraints: The active interval satisfies 0 <= left <= right.
Both boundaries fit in the fixed-width signed integer type.

options.text: (left + right) / 2 without any overflow consideration.
left * right / 2.
(right - left) / 2 without adding left.
left + (right - left) / 2.

feedback.reason: Computing the interval offset before adding it to left avoids summing two large boundaries.

blocks.text: With 0 <= left <= right and both boundaries representable, right - left is a nonnegative interval width that also fits the type. Integer division computes an offset no larger than that width, and left + offset stays between left and right. By contrast, left + right can overflow even when both endpoints and the true midpoint are valid.

blocks.title: Rounding must match progress
blocks.text: The formula shown is floor-biased. With closed exact-search updates mid ± 1, either adjacent state removes mid, so floor bias preserves progress.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_mid: The sum can overflow even when both boundaries are valid.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.product_mid: This is not the interval midpoint and can overflow more easily.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.difference_only: This yields an offset rather than the absolute midpoint index.

items.prompt: An exact search compares target with nums[mid] using an ordering inconsistent with how the array was sorted. What is the main defect?

options.text: The search remains correct but becomes slower.
The direction chosen after comparison no longer preserves the target-candidate invariant.
The defect appears only when duplicates exist.
The midpoint necessarily overflows.

feedback.reason: The search order and comparison relation must agree.

blocks.text: A branch is legal only because the comparator used during search describes the same ordering that arranged the array. If the array is descending but the code applies ascending rules, nums[mid] < target incorrectly moves right even though larger values lie left. The algorithm can then discard the target while still halving normally.

blocks.title: Fast progress can still be wrong
blocks.text: Strict interval shrink proves termination, not correctness. The sort relation, equality relation, and directional updates must form one consistent order contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_slower: An inconsistent comparator can discard the side containing the target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates_only: A descending array of distinct values already fails under ascending update rules; duplicates are not required for the contradiction.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_overflow: Midpoint overflow concerns boundary arithmetic, while this defect occurs after a valid mid because comparison direction contradicts sort order.

items.prompt: Which statements belong to the complete correctness-and-termination proof for classic exact search? Select all that apply.

options.text: If target exists, at least one matching index remains inside the active interval.
The interval always contains the first occurrence specifically.
Every discarded index is proven unable to contain target.
Every nonterminal update removes mid and strictly shrinks the interval.

feedback.reason: Classic exact search preserves possible membership and removes known-impossible regions.

blocks.text: The proof has two roles. The correctness invariant says every possible target index remains inside the active interval and every outside index was legally eliminated. The termination variant says every nonterminal mismatch removes mid and strictly reduces interval size. Together they prove the algorithm neither loses a possible answer nor loops forever.

blocks.title: Any-match is deliberately weaker
blocks.text: The proof preserves at least one matching index if any exists. It need not preserve the first occurrence specifically; that would require a strengthened boundary invariant and different equality branch.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_occurrence: That stronger boundary invariant is not required for any-match search.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.target_inside: This is the core candidate invariant: a legal update cannot discard every remaining occurrence of target.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.outside_eliminated: This records why shrinking is safe rather than merely fast: every removed index must be impossible under sorted order.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.strict_progress: This is the termination measure: excluding mid after a mismatch makes the finite interval strictly smaller.

items.prompt: Which test cases are important for classic exact binary search? Select all that apply.

options.text: Empty input.
Only one odd-length case where target starts at the midpoint.
A singleton containing and not containing target.
Target at the first and last index.

feedback.reason: Boundary, absence, and minimal-size cases expose most invariant defects.

blocks.text: Each accepted test isolates a different proof obligation. Empty input checks initialization and zero reads. Singleton hit and miss check whether a one-candidate interval is processed and then removed correctly. Targets at index 0 and n - 1 check that directional updates retain both closed endpoints.

blocks.title: A midpoint hit tests almost no movement
blocks.text: One odd-length case whose target starts at mid can succeed even if both update directions, endpoint handling, and not-found termination are wrong.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_middle: This does not exercise updates or edge boundaries.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.empty: It verifies that [0, -1] skips midpoint access and returns not found normally.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.singleton_hit_miss: The hit checks equality on left == right; the miss checks that the sole nonmatch is removed and terminates.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.target_edges: These cases expose updates that accidentally discard index 0 or n - 1 before inspection.

items.prompt: Which updates are valid for closed-interval exact search after a strict comparison? Select all that apply.

options.text: If nums[mid] < target, set left = mid + 1.
If nums[mid] < target, set left = mid.
If nums[mid] > target, set right = mid - 1.
If nums[mid] == target, return mid under an any-match contract.

feedback.reason: Each branch either returns a valid answer or removes the known-nonmatching midpoint with the impossible side.

blocks.text: Ascending order turns each strict comparison into a regional proof. If nums[mid] < target, every index through mid is too small, so left becomes mid + 1. If nums[mid] > target, every index from mid rightward is too large, so right becomes mid - 1. Equality already satisfies the any-match contract.

blocks.title: Why left = mid is invalid here
blocks.text: After a strict mismatch mid cannot be the answer. On a singleton interval, retaining mid leaves boundaries unchanged, so the algorithm loses its termination proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.too_small_keep_mid: Mid is known wrong and retaining it can stall on a singleton interval.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.too_small: Sorted order proves mid and every earlier value are below target, so none can remain a candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.too_large: Sorted order proves mid and every later value exceed target, so none can remain a candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.equal_return: nums[mid] == target supplies an existing matching index, exactly satisfying the any-match output contract.

items.prompt: Arrange one iteration of classic exact binary search.

elements.text: Confirm the active closed interval is non-empty.
Compute a midpoint inside the interval.
Return on equality; otherwise discard the proven-impossible side including mid.

feedback.reason: The update decision follows midpoint evidence inside a valid active interval.

blocks.text: Each operation depends on state established by the previous one: the interval must contain a candidate before mid can be indexed, and no branch can be chosen before comparing that candidate.

items: Confirm left <= right, so the closed interval contains at least one valid candidate index.
Compute a midpoint guaranteed to lie between left and right.
Compare nums[mid] with target under the same ordering used to sort the array.
Return mid on equality; otherwise use sorted order to remove mid and the proven-impossible half.

blocks.title: One iteration must either finish or progress
blocks.text: Every mismatch branch sets left = mid + 1 or right = mid - 1, preserving possible matches while strictly shrinking the interval.

items.prompt: Arrange the reasoning after nums[mid] is less than target in ascending data.

elements.text: Establish that mid is not a match and is too small.
Use sorted order to show every index at or left of mid is also too small.

feedback.reason: The boundary update is justified by a chain from local comparison to regional elimination.

blocks.text: The assignment left = mid + 1 is the conclusion of a proof, not a memorized direction. Each link must hold before the next one is legal.

items: Establish nums[mid] < target, so mid itself is not a match.
Use ascending order: for every j <= mid, nums[j] <= nums[mid] < target, so the entire left region is impossible.
Set left = mid + 1, excluding exactly the region just proven impossible.
Continue with [left, right], which still contains every possible target index and is strictly smaller.

blocks.title: Local comparison needs the order bridge
blocks.text: Without the second step, nums[mid] < target rules out only mid. Sorted order is what extends that fact to every earlier index.

items.prompt: Arrange the debugging steps for an exact search that misses a target at the final index.

elements.text: State whether the active interval is closed or half-open.
Trace the iteration where only the final index remains.
Verify that the loop condition still processes a one-element interval.
Verify earlier updates did not discard the final index incorrectly.

feedback.reason: Off-by-one debugging starts from the interval contract and the smallest failing state.

blocks.text: A final-index miss can arise either because an earlier update illegally excludes n - 1 or because the final singleton is reached but never processed. The audit order must distinguish those causes.

items: State the interval convention and its legal endpoints; for closed search, n - 1 starts inside [0, n - 1].
Trace left and right on the failing input, tracking whether the target index remains inside after every iteration.
For each update before failure, verify sorted order actually proves the target index belongs to the retained side.
If the target survives to left = right = n - 1, verify the loop uses left <= right and therefore inspects that singleton.

blocks.title: Fix the first broken invariant
blocks.text: Changing the loop condition cannot repair an earlier update that already discarded n - 1, and changing an update cannot repair a singleton skipped by left < right.

items.prompt: An iterative exact binary search runs on n sorted elements with Θ(1) work per iteration. Select its tightest offered worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds.
constraints: The active interval is reduced by about half after each mismatch.

feedback.reason: Strict interval halving gives logarithmic iterations, and iterative boundaries require constant extra state.

blocks.text: After k mismatches, at most about n/2^k candidates remain. Emptying a worst-case unsuccessful search requires k = Θ(log n), and Θ(1) work per iteration gives Θ(log n) total time, matching O(log n). The iterative implementation retains only a constant number of indices and temporary values, so auxiliary space is Θ(1), matching O(1).

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: Time O(1) is too small for worst-case halving; O(n) and O(n log n) are loose, not tight. Space O(log n), O(n), and O(n log n) overstate the constant iterative state. Sorting cost is excluded because input is already sorted.

items.prompt: A recursive exact binary search on n sorted elements performs Θ(1) work per call. Select its tightest offered worst-case time and recursion-stack-space bounds.
constraints: Each recursive call searches at most half of the previous interval.

feedback.reason: Recursive and iterative versions visit logarithmically many intervals, but recursion retains one frame per level.

blocks.text: The recurrence T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1) has depth Θ(log n), so worst-case time is Θ(log n), matching O(log n). Each call remains active until its child returns, leaving one constant-size frame per level; peak recursion-stack space is therefore Θ(log n), also matching O(log n).

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: Time O(1) is too small, while O(n) and O(n log n) are loose for halving. Recursion space is not O(1) because parent frames remain live, and O(n) or O(n log n) overstate logarithmic call depth.
